name: Rawdon, Quebec
note: Fishing locations for this city. Downloaded with the city's map, not bundled with the app. Every record here is marked unverified: the water, the species, the months and the hazards are researched, and the access scores and depth profiles are deliberately absent because inventing those is what gets somebody stuck in mud with nowhere to park. Zone 8 sets its periods and limits per waterbody rather than per zone, so the months given here are when the fish are catchable, NOT a statement that the water is open — look the water up by name in the zone 8 tool before you go.

spots.name: Lac Rawdon
spots.blurb: The lake the town sits on, and the one most people here fish first. Developed shoreline with cottages and docks most of the way round, a weedy shallow end and a deeper basin. A mixed warmwater lake rather than a trout lake — bass around the docks and the pads, perchaude everywhere, brochet on the weed edges.
spots.hazards: Almost the whole shoreline is private cottage land. Public access is limited to the municipal points, and walking somebody's lawn to reach the water is trespass whatever the map shows. Busy with boats and swimmers through July and August — fish it early or late.
spots.tip: The dock line is the fishery. Cast at the posts and the shade under the decks rather than at open water, and do it in the first and last hour of the day when the boat traffic has gone.

spots.name: Lac Pontbriand
spots.blurb: A smaller, quieter lake a few minutes north of town with less development than Lac Rawdon and colder water at the deep end. Panfish and brochet along the margins, and enough depth that brook trout hold through the summer where the springs come in.
spots.hazards: Shoreline cottages again, and the launch is small. The north end is shallow and weeds up badly by August. Cold water well into May — this lake warms later than it looks like it should.
spots.tip: Work the inflow at the north end in spring and autumn. That is where the cold water arrives and it is the only part of this lake worth a brook trout cast.

spots.name: Chutes Dorwin
spots.blurb: The waterfall park on the Ouareau, and the best-known piece of water in Rawdon for reasons that have nothing to do with fishing. Below the falls the river runs through a rocky gorge into a series of pools — cold, clean, boulder-strewn water that holds smallmouth in the pools and brook trout in the cold seams.
spots.hazards: A GORGE WITH A WATERFALL IN IT. The rock is slick with spray and moss year-round, the drop from the viewing areas is lethal, and people have died here. Stay on the marked trails and out of the water at the falls themselves. The park charges admission and has opening hours — this is not dawn-to-dark access.
spots.tip: Fish the pools well below the falls, not the plunge pool. Cast upstream into the head of a pool and let a tube jig come back with the current over the boulders.

spots.name: Lac Ouareau
spots.blurb: The big deep lake of the district, about an hour north into the Laurentians. Genuinely cold and deep enough to hold touladi through the summer, which none of the lakes nearer Rawdon can do. Also brochet in the bays and perchaude everywhere. This is the drive-out lake rather than the after-work one.
spots.hazards: Big water that builds a real chop when the wind comes down the length of it, and the shoreline is mostly rock with few places to get out. Cold enough year-round that going in is a serious matter. Boat access dominates; shore fishing is limited to the public points.
spots.tip: The touladi are a shore fish for two or three weeks after ice-out and then they are gone deep until autumn. If you are here in July, fish the bays for brochet instead and come back in May.

spots.name: Lac Maskinongé
spots.blurb: A large, relatively shallow and fertile lake east of Rawdon, and the walleye water of the district — doré jaune is what people come here for. Named for the maskinongé, which are still in it and still very hard to catch. Big weed flats, a soft bottom and enough size that the wind matters.
spots.hazards: Shallow and large, which is the combination that builds a short steep chop fast — this lake gets dangerous in a wind quicker than its size suggests. Weed growth is heavy from July. A summer town with a busy launch.
spots.tip: Doré water, and doré here means low light. Fish the last hour of the evening on the break where a flat drops into the basin, and measure everything: 37 to 53 cm goes back and that is most of what you will catch.

spots.name: Rivière L'Assomption at Joliette
spots.blurb: The main river of Lanaudière, running through Joliette with parks and a riverside path along a good stretch of it. Wider and slower than the Ouareau, with deep pools, current breaks and a mixed river fishery — doré and dorés noirs in the pools, smallmouth on the rock, and the occasional maskinongé that will ruin your tackle.
spots.hazards: Urban river with steep banks in places and a current that is stronger than the surface suggests after rain. Spring levels come up fast with the melt. Some stretches through town are park and some are private frontage — the path is not a right to the bank everywhere along it.
spots.tip: Fish the pools and the seams behind the current breaks, not the open flow. Cast upstream and let the bait come back naturally with the water.

spots.name: Rivière de l'Achigan
spots.blurb: A small river south-west of Rawdon that runs down to the Assomption, named for the bass in it. Much smaller water than the Assomption — a stream you can read from the bank. Smallmouth in the rocky runs, brook trout in the colder upper reaches, and enough shade that it fishes in summer when the lakes have gone flat.
spots.hazards: Runs mostly through farmland, so bank access is the road crossings and little else — walking a field to the water is trespass. Brush, undercut banks and agricultural runoff after heavy rain. Low and warm by late summer in the lower reaches.
spots.tip: Small water wants small tackle. A light spinner or a tube jig cast upstream into the head of each run, working downstream, will cover it properly in an afternoon.
